clinicalPearls: PD is the second most common age-related neurodegenerative disease after Alzheimer's; mean age of onset ~60 years, lifetime risk ~3% in men and ~2% in women, though cases can occur in the twenties or younger, particularly with a pathogenic gene mutation (p.3493).

Cardinal motor features are bradykinesia, rest tremor, rigidity, and gait dysfunction with postural instability; additional motor features include freezing of gait, micrographia, masked facies (hypomimia), reduced eye blinking, drooling, soft voice (hypophonia), and dysphagia (p.3493-3494).

Parkinsonism (bradykinesia with rigidity and/or tremor) combined with rest tremor, asymmetry of motor impairment, and a good levodopa response is much more likely to predict the correct pathologic diagnosis; with these U.K. Brain Bank Criteria, PD can be confirmed pathologically in >90% of patients (p.3495).
Levodopa is the gold standard symptomatic therapy; almost all PD patients improve, and failure to respond to an adequate trial of levodopa should cause the diagnosis to be questioned (p.3501).

Dopamine-system imaging (PET/SPECT) typically shows reduced, asymmetric striatal uptake, most pronounced in the posterior putamen with relative sparing of the caudate; it is useful when the diagnosis is uncertain but is not routinely required (p.3495-3496).
Among forms of parkinsonism, PD is the most common (~75% of cases) (p.3495).
harrison.pathophysiology: Pathologic hallmarks are degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), reduced striatal dopamine, and intraneuronal alpha-synuclein-staining inclusions in cell bodies and axons (Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites; collectively Lewy pathology). Lewy pathology can also affect cholinergic neurons of the nucleus basalis of Meynert, noradrenergic neurons of the locus coeruleus, serotonergic raphe neurons, and the olfactory system, cerebral hemispheres, spinal cord, and peripheral autonomic nervous system, accounting for nonmotor features. Pathology may begin in the peripheral autonomic nervous system, GI tract, olfactory system, or dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus and spread sequentially (Braak staging), giving rise to 'body-first' versus 'brain-first' concepts. In the basal-ganglia network, dopamine denervation leads to increased firing of the subthalamic nucleus (STN) and globus pallidus interna (GPi), excessive inhibition of the thalamus, reduced cortical motor activation, and the emergence of parkinsonian features. Pathogenesis involves an interacting network of oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, protein aggregation, excitotoxicity, and inflammation; a 'double hit' of genetic susceptibility plus an environmental insult has been proposed (p.3493-3494, p.3498-3500).
additionalDifferentials: Atypical parkinsonism: multiple-system atrophy (MSA) - cerebellar (MSA-c) and Parkinson (MSA-p) types
Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) - parkinsonian and Richardson variants
Dementia with Lewy bodies / PD with dementia

Secondary parkinsonism: drug-induced, tumor, infection, vascular, normal-pressure hydrocephalus, trauma, liver failure, toxins (carbon monoxide, manganese, MPTP, cyanide, hexane, methanol, carbon disulfide)
Essential tremor (high-frequency 6-10 Hz symmetric postural tremor with prominent kinetic component)
Huntington's disease (especially the juvenile Westphal variant)
Spinocerebellar ataxias and neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (e.g., PANK-associated neurodegeneration)
infectionMimics: Infection-related secondary parkinsonism (basal ganglia damage from CNS infection)

Post-influenza / postencephalitic parkinsonism (historical association with the influenza A epidemic); new-onset PD has been reported following SARS-CoV-2 infection, which can also worsen existing PD features
nonInfectiousMimics: Drug-induced parkinsonism - most commonly dopamine-blocking neuroleptics, and also metoclopramide (a neuroleptic agent used for GI problems), tetrabenazine, calcium channel blockers (flunarizine, cinnarizine), amiodarone, and lithium
Vascular parkinsonism (stroke affecting the SNc may closely resemble PD)
Toxin-induced parkinsonism (carbon monoxide or manganese damaging the globus pallidus resemble atypical parkinsonism with poor levodopa response)
additionalInvestigations: Dopamine-system imaging with PET or SPECT (reduced, asymmetric striatal/posterior-putamen uptake); not routinely required
Metabolic basal ganglia/thalamus imaging (18F-deoxyglucose) - may help distinguish atypical parkinsonism (decreased GPi with increased thalamic activity, the reverse of PD)

MRI - to evaluate for vascular/structural causes and atypical features (e.g., midbrain 'hummingbird sign' in PSP, putaminal rim change or pontine 'hot cross bun' sign in MSA); transcranial sonography or special MRI protocols may detect increased SNc iron
Alpha-synuclein seeding amplification assay (SAA) on CSF or skin - high sensitivity and specificity, can distinguish PD from other parkinsonisms (currently mainly research use)

Genetic testing - selective use for strong family history, early onset (<40 years), or particular ethnic backgrounds (GBA1, LRRK2, SNCA, etc.); monogenic forms account for ~5% of cases (~15% including GBA1 variants)
Serum/urinary copper studies to exclude Wilson's disease, which is treatable with copper chelators
redFlags: Early speech and gait impairment with early falls, lack of rest tremor, and lack of motor asymmetry - suggests atypical parkinsonism
Poor or no response to an adequate trial of levodopa - suggests atypical or secondary parkinsonism
Exposure to neuroleptics - suggests drug-induced parkinsonism
Onset before age 40 years - consider a genetic form of PD, Wilson's disease, or dopa-responsive dystonia
Liver disease - consider Wilson's disease or non-Wilsonian hepatolenticular degeneration
Hallucinations and dementia preceding or as the first/early feature - suggests dementia with Lewy bodies
Diplopia, impaired vertical gaze, slow saccades with impaired downgaze - suggests PSP
Prominent orthostatic hypotension or prominent cerebellar signs - suggests MSA
harrison.prognosis: PD is progressive. Levodopa prolongs independence and employability, improves quality of life, and increases life span, but chronic treatment with ongoing disease progression is associated in most patients with motor complications - response fluctuations ('on'/'off', wearing-off, on-off phenomenon) and dyskinesias. As the disease advances, nondopaminergic features that respond poorly to levodopa emerge - falling, freezing, autonomic dysfunction, sleep disorders, and dementia - and these (especially falls and dementia) are the primary source of disability and the main reason for hospitalization and nursing home placement in advanced PD. Atypical parkinsonisms generally follow a more aggressive course than classic PD (p.3496-3497, p.3501).
pitfalls: Diagnosing PD on two of three cardinal features alone carries a ~24% postmortem error rate; rest tremor, motor asymmetry, and a good levodopa response markedly improve diagnostic accuracy (p.3495).

Drug-induced parkinsonism is the most common secondary parkinsonism and is easily missed - remember that metoclopramide, used for GI symptoms, is a neuroleptic, and that calcium channel blockers (flunarizine, cinnarizine), tetrabenazine, amiodarone, and lithium can also be responsible (p.3497).
Wilson's disease must be actively excluded because progression can be prevented with copper chelators (p.3497).
Dopamine-system imaging cannot separate PD from atypical parkinsonism, since striatal dopamine depletion occurs in both (p.3496).
Some genetic forms of PD (e.g., certain LRRK2 cases) may occur without Lewy bodies, and MPTP toxicity causes parkinsonism typically without Lewy bodies (p.3496, p.3498).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison does not present a single formal severity grading; clinical diagnostic confidence is staged by the MDS Clinical Diagnostic Criteria into 'clinically established PD' and 'clinically probable PD', which combine core motor parkinsonism with supportive criteria, absolute exclusion criteria, and red flags. Disease evolution is commonly framed by the emergence of levodopa-related motor complications and levodopa-unresponsive nondopaminergic features in advanced PD (p.3495-3496, p.3501).
management: Use levodopa combined with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor as the mainstay symptomatic therapy, titrated to motor benefit
Employ dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors and COMT inhibitors as alternatives or adjuncts, particularly in younger patients or to smooth the motor response
Manage motor complications such as wearing-off, on-off fluctuations and dyskinesia by fractionating levodopa dosing and adding amantadine for dyskinesia
Offer advanced therapies for refractory fluctuations, including deep brain stimulation, continuous apomorphine infusion, or intestinal levodopa-carbidopa gel
Treat non-motor features with laxatives for constipation, measures for orthostatic hypotension, and quetiapine, clozapine or pimavanserin for psychosis while avoiding typical antipsychotics
Provide multidisciplinary rehabilitation with physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy for hypophonia and dysphagia, and a Parkinson's specialist nurse
Offer genetic counselling for early-onset or strongly familial disease such as GBA1 or LRRK2 variants
Monitor for progression, falls, cognitive decline and treatment side effects, escalating to palliative care in advanced disease
